description: We are a school team from Saudi Arabia: two Grade 5 students and their computer teacher. We built Mission Control Delay, a Scratch game where players drive a Mars rover while commands arrive late, showing why rovers need autonomy. We love space, coding and game design. Join us to help kids learn real space science through play! We are looking for members with skills in game art, sound design, Scratch or web coding, and science communication.
summary: Real Mars rovers cannot be driven live: a radio signal takes about 4 to 20 minutes to cross between Earth and Mars, because signals are fast but Mars is very far and both planets keep moving. Mission Control Delay lets young students feel this problem. As Mission Control, they write up to 10 commands for the fictional rover Noor, press SEND, wait for the delayed signal, and watch Noor obey with no chance to change the plan. Five levels add longer delays, rocks, pits and dust storms, using NASA dust-storm facts. An AUTONOMY switch lets Noor stop at danger, report "Obstacle ahead!" and find a safe path itself, showing why real rovers need autonomy. Made for primary students up to Grade 4, the Scratch game is bilingual (English and Arabic), shows a NASA "Did you know?" fact after each attempt, and logs every attempt so classes can compare results with autonomy on and off. Next, we will test it in classrooms and work with teachers and experts to grow it for more students.
details:
THE IDEA

A Mars rover cannot be steered live: every command from Earth takes roughly 4 to 20 minutes to arrive. Mission Control Delay lets students feel that problem. They play Mission Control, drive the rover Noor to a power station, and discover that a command sent late cannot be taken back.

TARGET AUDIENCE

Primary school students up to Grade 4, with teachers and parents. The game uses simple rules, large buttons, short sentences and two languages (English and Arabic, switchable at any time).

HOW IT PLAYS

Mission Control Delay is a Scratch 3 game where students act as Mission Control on Earth and drive a fictional Mars rover, Noor, to a power station. They write up to 10 commands (forward, left, right), press SEND, and wait. The list "travels" to Mars with a signal delay, then Noor follows it one step at a time and the plan cannot be changed. There are five levels: Level 1 has no delay; Level 2 has 3 seconds with rocks and a pit; Level 3 has 6 seconds and a dust storm that blocks column 5 at step 4; Levels 4 (8 seconds) and 5 (10 seconds) add more rocks, pits and a storm in a different column. If Noor hits something, a plain-language card explains why and shows a "Did you know?" fact.

AUTONOMY: THE ROVER THINKS FOR ITSELF

Switch Autonomy on and Noor checks each square itself. It stops, reports "Obstacle ahead!", then finds a safe path to the goal. If the storm has closed every route it stops safely, so autonomy helps but does not replace good planning. This is the idea behind real rover navigation.

LEARNING FROM EVERY ATTEMPT

Each attempt ends with a plain-language reason and a "Did you know?" fact based on NASA pages. Students practise sequencing, spatial reasoning and debugging a failed plan.

WHY IS THERE A DELAY?

The game explains the delay instead of only using it. Radio signals travel at the speed of light, which is very fast, but Mars is very far from Earth (on average about 140 million miles, according to NASA) and both planets keep moving. So a one-way signal takes about 4 to 20 minutes.

NASA DUST DATA INSIDE THE GAME

Levels 3 to 5 show NASA dust-storm facts on their cards and result cards: storms form in every Martian season and can grow in days; a 2022 storm was nearly twice the size of the United States; global storms come roughly every 5.5 years; in 2018 one ended the Opportunity rover's mission. The storm's column and timing in each level are our own design, inspired by these facts.

FUTURE WORK

1) Test with real classes and use the attempt logs to compare autonomy ON and OFF.

2) Talk to teachers and space-education organisations to improve and widen the project.

3) Add more levels and more real NASA dust and weather data.

4) Have the Arabic reviewed by native speakers and add more languages.

5) Grow the game for older students beyond Grade 4.

TOOLS AND USE OF AI

Built in Scratch 3 (core blocks only) and generated with Python, with Pillow and ffmpeg for the logo and video. The game is bilingual: English and Arabic. It turns a real mission problem, signal delay, into a puzzle where the enemy is time. Students plan ahead, then see how autonomy helps a rover protect itself. It builds sequencing, spatial reasoning and debugging, and logs every attempt so a class can run a small experiment.
